comments.text_zh: 人们经常问我：“这是 Dynabook 吗，那是 Dynabook 吗？”这个想法中只有大约 5% 在于外形包装（而且 1968 年除了平板这个想法之外，还考虑过另外两种不同的包装——来自 Ivan 的 HMD 想法，以及来自 Nicholas 的 ubiquitous 想法）。我做的几乎所有思考都基于 ARPA 社区已经完成的工作——以“服务”的形式呈现——并为儿童的世界重新塑造。这一切都非常直接地关乎 Steve 后来所说的“Wheels for the Mind”。如果有人有兴趣看看我们当时想法的一部分，几年前我们几个人，包括 Dan Ingalls，复活了 Xerox Parc 1978 年软件的一个版本，那是 Xerox 扔掉的东西（它是从垃圾堆里被救回来的）。这个系统正是 Steve Jobs 在 1979 年，也就是第二年访问时看到的那一版。我用这个系统为 Ted Nelson 致敬活动做了一个演示。它应该从 2:15 开始。看看你对 9:05 左右发生的事有什么想法。[VIDEO] 明年将是这个想法 50 周年，从那以后发生了很多事情，所以如果还回去鼓吹一套处于“可以花 10 年建成”语境下的想法，那会很疯狂；如果我们 30 年后还没有（那会是 1998 年，差不多 20 年前），那就很荒唐。ARPA/PARC 的大想法是：人类值得向往的未来将需要学习许多困难的东西，而不仅仅是阅读、写作和几道算术。如果“平等权利”要在整个星球上具有意义
comments.text: People often ask me "Is this a Dynabook, is that a Dynabook?". Only about 5% of the idea was in packaging (and there were 2 other different packages contemplated in 1968 besides the tablet idea -- the HMD idea from Ivan, and the ubiquitous idea from Nicholas). Almost all the thought I did was based on what had already been done in the ARPA community -- rendered as "services" -- and resculpted for the world of the child. It was all quite straightforwardly about what Steve later called "Wheels for the Mind". If people are interested to see part of what we had in mind, a few of us including Dan Ingalls a few years ago revived a version of the Xerox Parc software from 1978 that Xerox had thrown away (it was rescued from a trash heap). This system was the vintage that Steve Jobs saw the next year when he visited in 1979. I used this system to make a presentation for a Ted Nelson tribute. It should start at 2:15. See what you think about what happens around 9:05. comments.author: alankay
comments.story_title: Why OO Sucks by Joe Armstrong (2000)
comments.why_zh: NoteTaker Smalltalk-78 复活演示，约 10,000 行代码
comments.quote_zh: 我用它制作了向 Ted Nelson 致敬的视觉素材。看看你觉得怎么样。
comments.text_zh: 这跑出了本讨论串的范围，但我们当时相当确信，“仿真式”系统设计会是一种强大得多、也全面得多的方式，用来在计算机上创建大多数东西，尤其是在个人计算机上。在 Parc，我觉得我们证明了自己的观点。大约 2014 年，我们复活了 1978 年的 NoteTaker Smalltalk，我用它制作了向 Ted Nelson 致敬的视觉素材。看看你觉得怎么样。[VIDEO] 这个系统——包括所有东西——“OS”、SDK、Media、GUI、Tools 和内容——大约是 10,000 行 Smalltalk-78 代码，跑在大约 6K 字节的机器码之上（后者通过模拟来让整个系统跑起来）。我觉得发生的情况是，早期那些编程风格，尤其是“data structures、procedures、imperative munging 等”，被固守了下来，部分原因是这就是当时教的东西，而在 Parc 发展出的更重设计、同时也更紧凑的风格显得非常陌生。所以当 C++、Java 等出现时，旧风格被保留下来，class 则被降格为创建抽象数据类型，配上可以从外部摆弄的 getters 和 setters。注意，这也是“仿真式编程”，但模拟数据结构是一种很弱的设计方式，难以获得能力和扩展性。我觉得“所有实体都可以是受保护进程（而且双向受保护），并能作为构建系统的通信模块来使用”这个想法，既被错过了，也被拒绝了
comments.text: It's out of the context of this thread, but we were quite sure that "simulation-style" systems design would be a much more powerful and comprehensive way to create most things on a computer, and most especially for personal computers. At Parc, I think we were able to make our point. Around 2014 or so we brought back to life the NoteTaker Smalltalk from 1978, and I used it to make my visual material for a tribute to Ted Nelson. See what you think. [VIDEO] This system --including everything -- "OS", SDK, Media, GUI, Tools, and the content -- is about 10,000 lines of Smalltalk-78 code sitting on top of about 6K bytes of machine code (the latter was emulated to get the whole system going). I think what happened is that the early styles of programming, especially "data structures, procedures, imperative munging, etc." were clung to, in part because this was what was taught, and the more design-intensive but also more compact styles developed at Parc seemed very foreign. So when C++, Java, etc. came along the old styles were retained, and classes were relegated to creating abstract data types with getters and setters that could be munged from the outside. Note that this is also "simulation style programming" but simulating data structures is a very weak approach to design for power and scaling. I think the idea that all entities could be protected processes (and protected in both directions) that could be used as communicating modules for building systems got both missed and reject

comments.story_title: Emacs Is Not Enough
comments.why_zh: 展示了 1970 年代桌面计算更可组合的方向
comments.quote_zh: 我总是感慨，70 年代桌面计算机所走的有用方向
comments.text_zh: 每次看到这样的东西，我也会想起几年前 Xerox Alto 的那个演示。我会链接到最相关片段的开始处：[VIDEO] 我总是感慨，70 年代桌面计算机所走的有用方向，以及计算本可以比现在好得多。但我们早已彻底偏离了这一切，远离可组合性，转向彼此完全无法通信的独立盒子（“应用程序”）。Emacs 在某种程度上是我们今天朝另一个方向拥有的最好的东西，但与本来可能做到的事情相比，它黯然失色。
comments.text: Every time I see something like this, I'm also reminded of this demo of the Xerox Alto from a few years back. I'll link to the start of the most relevant piece: [VIDEO] I'm always struck by the useful directions that desktop computers were going in the 70s, and how computing could be so much better than it is right now. But we've veered so off-course from all of this, away from composability and towards independent boxes ("applications") that can't talk to each other at all. Emacs is in some ways the best thing we have today in the other direction, but it pales in comparison to what's possible.

comments.text_zh: 我喜欢这个概念试图把内容和应用分开。自从我看到早期 GUI 与今天的 GUI 有所不同的一些方式后，我就一直觉得，今天桌面上的应用彼此完全隔离，这种方式让我们失去了某些东西。Alto 让你可以实时地从多个窗口组合数据，有点像 shell 管道为命令行应用所做的那样：[VIDEO] 这个概念里的 Locus 和 Flows 似乎能够支持类似的工作流，因为数据不会像通常那样被限制在“应用”里。
comments.text: I love that this concept tries to separate content from apps. Ever since I saw some of the ways early GUIs differed from today's, I've had a feeling that we've lost something with the way apps in today's desktops are completely isolated from each other. The Alto let you compose data live from multiple windows kind of like a shell pipeline does for command-line apps: [VIDEO] The Locus and Flows in this concept seem like they could enable a similar workflow, as data isn't confined to "apps" the way it usually would be.

comments.text: When I write code it is usually either "kiddicode" for future "kiddilanguages" or "metacode" (for future languages ".") I did have a lot of fun last year writing code in a resurrected version of the Notetaker Smalltalk-78 (done mostly by Dan Ingalls and Bert Freudenberg from a rescued disk pack that Xerox had thrown away) to create a visual presentation for a tribute to Ted Nelson on his 70th birthday: [VIDEO] This particular system was a wonderful sweet spot for those days -- it was hugely expressive and quite small and understandable (my size). comments.text_zh: 没错，这种孤岛化也让我无法使用各个应用和格式自身“原生”的标注功能。相反，我更愿意把信息从这些孤岛（应用、格式等）里抽出来，放进我的笔记系统。这样我就能按自己的方式来高亮、标注等，也能获得集中化带来的好处，比如搜索和链接（楼主还有另一篇帖子描述自己的系统，挺酷的[1]）。目前我在用 Notion，它本身也是一个孤岛，但它让我能很大程度控制信息如何组织（也给了我一条逃离它的路线）。关于数据孤岛和围墙花园这个问题有很多视角。但我认为，对我们这些“终端用户”来说，这是一种相当糟糕的状态。对我来说，计算机意味着无限的灵活性和可塑性，但讽刺的是，我们用于标注和再混合的工具在实践中比物理世界里的还差。在物理世界里读一本书，我只要用铅笔在页边写批注，就能和作者对话。它流畅、直观，而且纸张这种媒介鼓励这样做（事实上它无法不被我的使用改变！页面会弯、会脏、会撕破等）。如果我想更进一步，可以加便利贴标出有趣的段落，可以复印几页做出小节，如果是杂志，我干脆把它们全撕下来！这种灵活性在电脑上就是没有。我觉得值得认真想想，为什么我们
comments.text: Yes, this siloing stops me from using annotation features "native" to each app and format as such as well. Instead, I prefer to exfiltrate information from the silos(apps, formats, etc) and put them into my note taking system. Then I can do highlights, annotations, etc. on my own terms and also get the benefits of centralization such as searching and linking(the OP has another post describing their own system, which is pretty cool[1]). Currently I'm using Notion, which is also a silo of its own, but it's one that gives me a lot of control over how I lay my information out(and an escape plan from). There are a lot of perspectives on this issue with data silos and walled gardens. But I'm of the opinion that it's a fairly bad state for all of us "end users". Computers to me are about infinite flexibility and malleability, but ironically the tools we have for annotation and remixing are in practice worse than what we have in the physical world. Reading a book in the physical world, I can converse with the author simply by jotting marginalia with my pencil. It's fluid, intuitive, and the medium of paper encourages it(in fact it can't help but be mutated by my use!: pages get bended, stained, torn, etc.). If I want to go further I can add post-it notes to mark interesting passages, I can xerox some pages and create subsections, if it's a magazine I can just tear them all out! comments.author: seltzered_
comments.story_title: Technology as It Should Be
comments.text_zh: “在《想象一个没有应用的世界》中，Shira Ovide 问了一个‘疯狂的问题：如果我们在智能手机上玩游戏、购物、看 Netflix、读新闻——却不用应用，会怎样？我们的智能手机，就像我们的电脑一样，将主要成为通过网页浏览器上网的入口。’这个问题可以外推成一个更大的问题：‘我们想从技术中得到什么？’”引用 Bret Victor 的话说，“要工具包，不要应用”：[LINK] [VIDEO] 直接跳到谈论提供商、个人数据、安全等等，预设了围绕设备存在‘个人’的文化脚手架。这没问题，但这个预设需要被意识到。
comments.text: "In Imagine a world without apps Shira Ovide asks “a wild question: What if we played games, shopped, watched Netflix and read news on our smartphones — without using apps? Our smartphones, like our computers, would instead mostly be gateways to go online through a web browser.” This question can be extrapolated into a larger question: “What do we want from our technology?"" To quote Bret Victor, "Toolkits, not Apps" : [LINK] [VIDEO] Jumping straight into talk about providers, personal data, security, etc. assumes cultural scaffolds of 'personal' around the device. That's fine, but the assumption needs to be made aware.

comments.author: morphle
comments.story_title: Alan Kay on “Should web browsers have stuck to being document viewers?” and ...
comments.text_zh: Alan Kay 在给 University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign 计算机科学学生做的讲座“Normal Considered Harmful”中，长篇大论地尖锐批评了 World Wide Web 浏览器（重新发明一个坏掉的轮子）。背景是：Alan 本人在 Xerox PARC 发明了 WYSIWYG。他亲临了 Douglas Englebart 的“所有演示之母”。发明超链接和 Xanadu 的 Ted Nelson 让 Alan 认识了他未来的妻子 [2]；而且当 Bill Atkinson 做出 Hypercard 时，Alan 就在 Apple。他提到，当他告诉 Tim Berners Lee，Douglas Englebart 做了好得多的工作时，Tim 感到懊恼（懊恼自己没读过任何论文，那些论文讲的是比 WWW 浏览器早 28 年、25 年和 20 年的更早且好得多的设计）。当然，Alan 也讨论了 Web 本来应该怎么做。简而言之，应该是当你点击一个超链接时，你在操作系统内核的安全沙箱里加载一个虚拟机。然后这个虚拟机会渲染（位图或矢量）页面。这是操作系统入门课的内容，1965 年就已广为人知。当然，Alan 的团队确实（多次）实现了这一点。如果你联系我，我可以演示这个。发邮件到 morphle [at] ziggo [dot] nl，我可以给你一段视频，内容是 Alan Kay、Douglas Englebart 和 Tim Berners Lee 在一个论坛讨论上碰面并谈论此事。你可以问我任何与 Alan、Ted 或 Douglas 相关的事情，我维护着一个庞大的档案库，里面有所有科学论文、电子邮件、演讲、采访和讲座视频。Alan、Ted 和 Douglas 曾密切合作
comments.text: Alan Kay made scathing comments on the World Wide Web browser (reinventing a broken wheel) at length in a lecture "Normal Considered Harmful" for computer science students at University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. For context: Alan himself invented WYSIWYG at Xerox PARC. He was present at "the mother of all demo's" by Douglas Englebart. Ted Nelson who invented hyperlinks and Xanadu got Alan in touch with his future wife [2] and Alan was there at Apple when Bill Atkinson made Hypercard. He mentions that when he told Tim Berners Lee about the much better work of Douglas Englebart, Tim was chagrined (that he had not read any of the papers about earlier and much better designs of 28, 25 and 20 years before the WWW browser). Of course Alan also discusses how the web should have been done. In short, it should be that when you click a hyperlink you load a virtual machine in a secure sandbox of a Operating System Kernel. The virtual machine would then render the (bitmap or vector) pages. Operating System 101, well known in 1965. Of course, Alan's team did implement this (several times). I can demo this if you contact me. Email me at morphle [at] ziggo [dot] nl for a video where Alan Kay, Douglas Englebart and Tim Berners Lee meet and talk about this at a forum discussion. You can ask me about anything related to Alan, Ted or Douglas, I maintain an extensive archive with all scientific papers, emails, talks, interviews and lecture video's.
